TextView.android:text: Operating Systems • Java & Kotlin Interop • Functions vs. Listeners

• Listener (OOP Pattern): An interface declaring callback contracts (e.g., BenchmarkListener.java). A background thread invokes listener methods upon reaching execution milestones, decoupling thread logic from the caller.

• Function (Functional Paradigm): A first-class citizen in Kotlin representing an executable block with input arguments and a return value.

• The Bridge (SAM Conversion): Single Abstract Method interfaces (e.g., BenchmarkProgressListener.java) allow Kotlin to seamlessly convert a lambda function into a Java listener instance:
 Kotlin: engine.setOnProgressListener { info -> updateUI(info) }
 Java: engine.setOnProgressListener(new BenchmarkProgressListener() { ... })

• Thread Boundaries: In Android, background threads cannot update the UI. The listener pattern dispatches events from worker threads across the OS thread boundary to the Main UI Looper via runOnUiThread.

• Java Engine (CpuBenchmarkEngine.java):
 Implements multi-threading with java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService, AtomicLong synchronization, and probes Linux kernel stats (/proc/self/task/TID/stat).

• Kotlin UI & Workload (MainActivity.kt, Workload.kt):
 Manages reactive UI updates, MPAndroidChart rendering, and Kotlin high-level math workloads.

• Bi-directional Interop:
 Kotlin code transparently calls Java classes, while Java threads fire callbacks that Kotlin lambdas handle smoothly.

• Linux Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS):
 Android user threads map 1-to-1 to Linux kernel tasks. CFS allocates CPU time proportional to thread nice values (-20 highest priority to +19 lowest priority).

• Core Detection:
 Field 39 of /proc/self/task/TID/stat reports the exact CPU core the thread last executed on. Our app samples this to dynamically highlight active CPU cores.

• Thread vs. Process Scheduling:
 Threads share the same virtual address space, memory heap, and open files (PID is shared, TIDs differ). Processes have isolated memory spaces and page tables, incurring higher context-switch overhead.

• Amdahl's Law: Speedup S(N) = 1 / ((1 - P) + P/N).
 Even with infinite CPU cores, the speedup is bounded by 1 / (1 - P). For example, if 10% of a workload is serial, speedup cannot exceed 10x.

• Race Conditions: Unsynchronized counter updates (total++) involve a three-step cycle: READ, MODIFY, WRITE. Concurrent threads interleave these steps, overwriting each other's updates. Synchronization via AtomicLong ensures hardware-level atomic instructions (CAS - Compare-And-Swap).
